vjimc-2026-cat2-01.title: Telescoping
vjimc-2026-cat2-01.body:
For every $x$,
$$\sin^2x-\tfrac14\sin^2 2x=\sin^2x-\sin^2x\cos^2x=\sin^2x\,(1-\cos^2x)=\sin^4x .$$
With $x=2^{-n}\alpha$ and multiplying by $4^n$:
$$4^n\sin^4(2^{-n}\alpha)=4^n\sin^2(2^{-n}\alpha)-4^{n-1}\sin^2(2^{-(n-1)}\alpha).$$
Summing for $n=1,\dots,N$, the sum telescopes:
$$\sum_{n=1}^N4^n\sin^4(2^{-n}\alpha)=4^N\sin^2(2^{-N}\alpha)-\sin^2\alpha .$$
As $N\to\infty$, $4^N\sin^2(2^{-N}\alpha)=\alpha^2\left(\frac{\sin(2^{-N}\alpha)}{2^{-N}\alpha}\right)^2\to\alpha^2$ (for $\alpha\ne0$; for $\alpha=0$ everything is $0$). Hence
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}4^n\sin^4(2^{-n}\alpha)=\alpha^2-\sin^2\alpha .$$
(Numerical check: for $\alpha=1$ both sides equal $0.29192658\ldots$; for $\alpha=10$ both equal $99.70404\ldots$.)

**Answer:** $\alpha^2-\sin^2\alpha$. ∎

vjimc-2026-cat2-01.title: A functional equation for the sum
vjimc-2026-cat2-01.body:
Let $F(\alpha)=\sum_{n\ge1}4^n\sin^4(2^{-n}\alpha)$; it converges since $|\sin t|\le|t|$ gives terms $\le\alpha^4/4^n$, and $|F(\alpha)|\le\alpha^4\sum4^{-n}=\alpha^4/3$. Shifting the index,
$$F(2\alpha)=\sum_{n\ge1}4^n\sin^4(2^{-(n-1)}\alpha)=4\sin^4\alpha+4F(\alpha).$$
Let $G(\alpha)=\alpha^2-\sin^2\alpha-F(\alpha)$. Using $\sin^22\alpha=4\sin^2\alpha\cos^2\alpha$,
$$G(2\alpha)=4\alpha^2-4\sin^2\alpha\cos^2\alpha-4\sin^4\alpha-4F(\alpha)=4\alpha^2-4\sin^2\alpha-4F(\alpha)=4G(\alpha).$$
Hence $G(\alpha)=4^mG(2^{-m}\alpha)$ for all $m$. Since $0\le t^2-\sin^2t\le t^4/3$ (from $t-\frac{t^3}6\le\sin t\le t$ for $t\ge0$ and parity) and $|F(t)|\le t^4/3$, we have $|G(t)|\le\frac23t^4$, so
$$|G(\alpha)|\le4^m\cdot\tfrac23\,\frac{\alpha^4}{16^m}\to0 .$$
Thus $G\equiv0$ and $F(\alpha)=\alpha^2-\sin^2\alpha$. ∎

vjimc-2026-cat2-02.title: Commuting with the diagonal matrix
vjimc-2026-cat2-02.body:
Let $D=\operatorname{diag}(n,1,-1,\dots,1,-1)$ and $p(x)=1+x+\dots+x^k$, so $p(A)=D$. Write $m=\frac{n-1}2$ (the number of $1$'s, and of $-1$'s, among the last $n-1$ entries).

**Case $n=1$.** Then $D=(1)$ and $\operatorname{tr}A=0$ forces $A=(0)$; indeed $p(0)=1$ and $\operatorname{tr}(A^{k+1})=0=n^2-1$. So $A=(0)$ for every $k$.

**Case $n\ge3$.** Then the eigenvalues $n,1,-1$ of $D$ are distinct.

*Block structure.* $A$ commutes with $p(A)=D$, so $A$ maps each eigenspace of $D$ into itself: $E_n=\operatorname{span}(e_1)$, $E_1=\operatorname{span}(e_2,e_4,\dots)$, $E_{-1}=\operatorname{span}(e_3,e_5,\dots)$. Thus, after grouping coordinates, $A=(a)\oplus B\oplus C$ with a real number $a$ and real $m\times m$ matrices $B,C$, and
$$p(a)=n,\qquad p(B)=I,\qquad p(C)=-I .$$

*Trace of $A^{k+1}$.* From $(A-I)p(A)=A^{k+1}-I$ we get $A^{k+1}=I+(A-I)D$, so
$$\operatorname{tr}(A^{k+1})=n+\operatorname{tr}(AD)-\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{tr}(AD)=na+\operatorname{tr}B-\operatorname{tr}C,$$
using $\operatorname{tr}D=n+m-m=n$. Together with $\operatorname{tr}A=a+\operatorname{tr}B+\operatorname{tr}C=0$, adding the two conditions gives $(n+1)a+2\operatorname{tr}B=n^2-1$, i.e.
$$a=n-1-\frac{2\operatorname{tr}B}{n+1}. \tag{1}$$

*Bound on $\operatorname{tr}B$.* $p(B)-I=B(I+B+\dots+B^{k-1})=0$, so each (complex) eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $B$ is $0$ or satisfies $1+\lambda+\dots+\lambda^{k-1}=0$, i.e. $\lambda^k=1$, $\lambda\ne1$. In all cases $|\lambda|\le1$, so $|\operatorname{tr}B|\le m=\frac{n-1}2$. By (1),
$$a\ge n-1-\frac{n-1}{n+1}>n-2\ge1 .$$

*$k\ge2$ is impossible.* Then $p(a)\ge1+a+a^2>1+(n-2)+1=n$ (using $a>n-2$ and $a^2>1$), contradicting $p(a)=n$.

*$k=1$.* Then $I+A=D$, i.e. $A=D-I=\operatorname{diag}(n-1,0,-2,0,-2,\dots,0,-2)$. It does satisfy the trace conditions:
$$\operatorname{tr}A=(n-1)-2m=0,\qquad \operatorname{tr}A^2=(n-1)^2+4m=(n-1)^2+2(n-1)=n^2-1 .$$

**Answer.** For $n\ge3$: if $k=1$ the unique matrix is $A=\operatorname{diag}(n-1,0,-2,0,-2,\dots,0,-2)$; if $k\ge2$ there is no such matrix. (For $n=1$ the only matrix is $A=(0)$, for every $k$; it agrees with $D-I$.) ∎

vjimc-2026-cat2-03.title: Size versus radical
vjimc-2026-cat2-03.body:
Put $s=x+y$. By definition $xz=s^n-y^n-x$, i.e.
$$s^n=xz+(x+y^n).$$
Since $z\mid x+y^n$, it follows that $z\mid s^n$. In particular every prime divisor of $z$ divides $s$.

**$z$ is large.** Since $s-y=x$,
$$z+1=\frac{s^n-y^n}{s-y}=s^{n-1}+s^{n-2}y+\dots+sy^{n-2}+y^{n-1}.$$
For $n\ge3$ the sum contains, besides $s^{n-1}$, at least the two terms $s^{n-2}y\ge1$ and $y^{n-1}\ge1$, so $z+1\ge s^{n-1}+2$, i.e.
$$z>s^{n-1}.$$

**Conclusion.** Suppose that no prime $p$ satisfies $p^n\mid z$. Then every prime appears in $z$ with exponent at most $n-1$, and all primes of $z$ divide $s$, so
$$z\le\prod_{p\mid z}p^{\,n-1}\le\Big(\prod_{p\mid s}p\Big)^{n-1}\le s^{n-1},$$
contradicting $z>s^{n-1}$. Hence some prime $p$ (an integer $>1$) has $p^n\mid z$. ∎

*Remarks.* (1) The hypothesis $n>2$ is needed: for $n=2$, $y=1$ we get $z=x+1$, which always divides $x+y^2=x+1$, and $z$ need not have a square factor. (2) Example: $n=3$, $x=3$, $y=5$ gives $z=128=2^7$, which divides $x+y^3=128$.

vjimc-2026-cat2-04.title: Hyperbolic area counting
vjimc-2026-cat2-04.body:
**Interpretation.** As in the picture, the tiles are understood to be compact polygons: each tile is bounded by finitely many arcs and its corners lie inside the open disk. (Some such assumption is needed: the Farey tessellation by ideal triangles satisfies both bullet points but has no point of the open disk where three tiles meet, so it has no vertices at all.) If $O$ is a vertex, the product is $0$ trivially, so assume $|OV_k|>0$ for all $k$.

**Hyperbolic geometry.** Equip the disk with the Poincaré metric $ds=\frac{2|dz|}{1-|z|^2}$. Circle arcs perpendicular to the unit circle are its geodesics, and inversion in such a circle is an isometry. Write $\rho(P)$ for the hyperbolic distance from $O$; then $|OP|=\tanh\frac{\rho(P)}2$, so
$$1-|OP|=\frac{2}{e^{\rho(P)}+1}\ge e^{-\rho(P)}. \tag{1}$$
The hyperbolic disk $B(t)$ of radius $t$ about $O$ has area $4\pi\sinh^2\frac t2=2\pi(\cosh t-1)$.

**All tiles are congruent.** Neighbouring tiles are images of each other under an isometry, and any two tiles are joined by a chain of neighbours, so every tile is isometric to a fixed tile $T$. Let $\mathcal A>0$ be its area and $D<\infty$ its diameter, and let $\theta>0$ be its smallest interior angle.

**Each tile has a vertex, and each vertex lies on few tiles.** Let $P$ be a corner of a tile $T'$, where two sides of $T'$ meet at an angle $<\pi$. If only two tiles met at $P$, then near $P$ the boundary of $T'$ would be a single common boundary arc — not a corner. So at least three tiles meet at $P$: every tile has at least one vertex of the tessellation on its boundary. Conversely, the tiles at a vertex $V$ have disjoint interiors and each occupies an angle $\ge\theta$ at $V$, so at most $N=\lfloor2\pi/\theta\rfloor$ tiles contain $V$.

**Counting vertices.** Let $M(t)$ be the number of vertices with $\rho(V_k)\le t$. (If $M(t)=\infty$ for some $t$, infinitely many $|OV_k|$ are $\le\tanh\frac t2<1$, and the product is $0$; so assume all $M(t)$ finite.) The tiles meeting $B(t-D)$ cover it, so there are at least $\operatorname{area}B(t-D)/\mathcal A$ of them; each lies inside $B(t)$ and has a vertex there; each vertex is counted at most $N$ times. Hence for $t>D$
$$M(t)\ge\frac{2\pi(\cosh(t-D)-1)}{N\mathcal A}\ge c\,e^{t}-C,\qquad c=\frac{\pi e^{-D}}{N\mathcal A}>0 .$$

**Divergence.** Writing $e^{-\rho}=\int_\rho^\infty e^{-t}\,dt$ and exchanging sum and integral (all terms are non-negative),
$$\sum_k e^{-\rho(V_k)}=\int_0^\infty e^{-t}M(t)\,dt\ \ge\int_{D+1}^\infty e^{-t}\big(ce^t-C\big)\,dt=\infty .$$

**Conclusion.** By (1) and $-\ln r\ge1-r$, with $r_k=|OV_k|\in(0,1)$,
$$\sum_k(-\ln r_k)\ge\sum_k(1-r_k)\ge\sum_ke^{-\rho(V_k)}=\infty .$$
The partial products $\prod_{k\le K}r_k=\exp\big(-\sum_{k\le K}(-\ln r_k)\big)$ therefore tend to $0$ (in any order of the vertices), i.e. $\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}|OV_k|=0$. ∎
